prompt: A regional insurer receives about 2,000 first-notice-of-loss emails a day. For each one the team wants to extract the policy number, loss date and loss type, look the policy up in the claims system, and file a structured claim record. The steps are the same for every email and the business wants per-step audit logs. Which architecture fits best?

options.text: A fixed workflow of sequenced model calls, with the policy lookup done in code between steps
An autonomous agent that reads each email, picks the tools it needs and plans its own sequence of actions
An orchestrator model that spawns one specialist agent per field to extract and then merges their outputs
A single prompt holding the email, the full claims schema and the entire policy register, answered in one call

explanation: Correct: A. The task is fully known in advance and never branches, so a fixed workflow (prompt chaining) gives predictable behaviour, a log line per step and a cheap place to validate between steps. B spends tokens and risk on planning a path that is already known. C adds multi-agent coordination for a three-field extraction that one call handles well. D stuffs the whole policy register into context on every email, which is slow, expensive and impossible to audit step by step.

prompt: A law firm wants an assistant that answers partners' questions about ongoing matters. Some questions need one document lookup, others need a dozen searches across filings, a date calculation and a draft memo, and the path is only clear once early results come back. Which pattern should the architect start from?

options.text: A routing workflow that classifies each question and dispatches it to one of four hand-built pipelines
A parallel workflow that runs every search the firm supports at once and has the model merge the results
An agent loop that calls search and calculation tools, observes results and decides the next step
A prompt chain with a fixed sequence of search, calculate and draft steps applied to every question

explanation: Correct: C. When the number and order of steps depend on what earlier steps reveal, an agent that acts, observes tool results and re-plans is the pattern that fits; the stopping condition and tool budget are then the controls to design. A works when the set of paths is small and known, which is not the case here. B wastes calls on searches that most questions do not need. D cannot adapt when a search turns up nothing or something unexpected.

prompt: A bank's customer-messaging assistant receives a mix of balance questions, fraud reports, mortgage enquiries and complaints. Each type needs different tools, a different tone and different escalation rules, and the team wants to tune one type without regressing the others. Which workflow pattern addresses this most directly?

options.text: Evaluator-optimizer: one model drafts the reply and a second critiques it until it passes the rules
Prompt chaining: each message passes through tone, tools and escalation steps in one fixed order
Parallelisation: all four specialist prompts answer every message and the best reply is chosen by vote
Routing: a first call classifies the message and hands it to a prompt and tool set built for that type

explanation: Correct: D. Routing separates concerns: each downstream prompt stays small and specific, and changing the complaints handler cannot affect the mortgage handler. A improves the quality of one reply but does not separate the four cases. C quadruples cost and lets the wrong specialist's tools run on every message. B forces a single sequence onto messages that need different tools and rules.

prompt: A pharmaceutical company asks Claude to review 300-page clinical study reports against a 70-item regulatory checklist in a single call. Reviewers find that items near the end of the checklist are often skipped and that findings are inconsistent between runs. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Raise the temperature so the model explores the checklist more thoroughly on each run
Have the model restate all 70 checklist items before it begins so that none of them are forgotten
Move the single-call design to a larger model with a longer context window
Split the review into calls per checklist section over the relevant report parts

explanation: Correct: D. Skipped late items and run-to-run variance are the classic signs of a task that is too large for one pass. Decomposing by checklist section (a sectioning form of parallelisation) gives each call a bounded job, makes the output comparable between runs and lets each section be evaluated on its own. A adds randomness, the opposite of consistency. B spends tokens restating the checklist without reducing the work per call. C may help at the margin but leaves the structural overload in place.

prompt: A travel company's booking agent must coordinate flight search, hotel search, visa checks and payment. Each sub-task needs its own tools and a long domain prompt, and the business wants the orchestration logic to be visible and testable in code rather than left to the model. Which design meets this?

options.text: A single agent with all the tools registered and one system prompt that covers all four domains
Four independent agents that watch a shared message queue and act when they see a relevant task
An orchestrator in application code that calls four specialist sub-agents in sequence with scoped context
A supervisor model given the four sub-agents as tools, deciding at runtime which to call and in what order

explanation: Correct: C. When the business wants orchestration that is inspectable and unit-testable, put the control flow in code and keep the model inside each specialist step; each sub-agent sees a narrow context, which also improves tool selection. A reproduces the bloated-context problem that decomposition is meant to solve. B makes the sequence emergent and hard to reason about or test. D is a legitimate orchestrator-workers pattern, but it moves the control flow into the model, which is exactly what the requirement rules out.

prompt: A research-synthesis product uses an orchestrator model that breaks a question into sub-questions, spawns a worker per sub-question, and writes the final report. Reports are good but cost has tripled since launch, and traces show workers repeatedly fetching the same sources. Which change best addresses the cost without changing the pattern?

options.text: Give the orchestrator a shared results store and dedupe sub-questions before spawning
Replace the workers with a single model call that answers every sub-question in one pass
Lower each worker's maximum output tokens so that the repeated fetches cost less per worker
Switch the orchestrator to the smallest model so that planning and decomposition cost less per report

explanation: Correct: A. The waste is duplicated work between workers, so the fix is shared state and deduplication at the orchestration layer; the orchestrator-workers shape stays intact. B abandons the pattern and reintroduces the overload that motivated it. C trims output, but the duplicated fetches are input and tool cost, not output. D saves little, because the orchestrator makes few calls, and risks worse decomposition, which produces more duplicated work rather than less.

prompt: A utility company's chief operating officer lists nine possible first AI projects, from an internal policy chatbot to automated outage-cause analysis. What should most strongly determine which project the architect recommends first?

options.text: Which project exercises the newest model capabilities, so the team learns the most from it
Which project the executive sponsor is personally most enthusiastic about championing
Which project has a measurable outcome, available data and a tolerable cost of error
Which project can run fully automated with no human review step in the loop at all

explanation: Correct: C. A first project should be one where value can be measured, the data exists, and a wrong answer is recoverable; that is what lets the organisation learn and build trust. A optimises for novelty, not value. B matters for sponsorship but is not the primary selection criterion. D treats removing humans as the goal, which raises risk on the very first delivery.

prompt: A procurement assistant has been live for a quarter. Dashboards show cost, latency and uptime, but nobody can say whether its supplier recommendations are being accepted or overridden by buyers. Which addition completes the architecture?

options.text: A feedback loop capturing buyer accept/override decisions into the evaluation set and prompt iteration
A second model that re-scores each recommendation independently and flags any disagreements for review
A larger context window so the assistant can see more supplier history on every single request
A weekly export of all prompts and responses to the data team for long-term archiving and reporting

explanation: Correct: A. An end-to-end architecture runs input, processing, output and a feedback loop; without the loop the team cannot learn whether outputs are right in production. B adds a second opinion but still never learns what buyers actually did. C changes inputs without measuring outcomes. D stores data but creates no signal or loop back into the system.

prompt: A manufacturer wants Claude to answer engineers' questions about 40,000 maintenance manuals that are updated by suppliers every month. Which approach gives the model access to this material in a way that stays current?

options.text: Fine-tune a model on the manuals and retrain it each time a supplier sends an updated manual
An augmented LLM that retrieves relevant manual sections at query time from a refreshed index
Summarise all the manuals into one 150,000-token document and place it in every system prompt
Ask engineers to paste the relevant manual pages into the conversation alongside each question they ask

explanation: Correct: B. Retrieval over a refreshed index is the standard way to give a model large, changing knowledge: the model sees only what is relevant and the index, not the model, is what gets updated. A bakes knowledge into weights that go stale monthly and is costly to repeat. C cannot hold 40,000 manuals and loses detail in the summary. D moves the retrieval problem onto the user.

prompt: A single internal agent handles facilities requests, expense queries and software access requests. It has 40 tools and a 7,000-token system prompt, and it has started picking the wrong tool as capabilities were added. What should the architect do?

options.text: Add a sentence to the system prompt listing which of the 40 tools belong to which of the three domains
Split the agent by domain behind a router, each specialist carrying only its own tools and prompt
Increase the maximum number of tool-use turns so the agent can recover after a wrong first tool choice
Rename every tool with a domain prefix such as `hr_` or `it_` and keep the single agent as it is

explanation: Correct: B. Tool-selection accuracy degrades as a tool set grows and overlaps; decomposing by domain shrinks each agent's choice set and prompt, which fixes the cause. A and D are prompt-level patches that leave 40 tools in every call. C makes wrong choices cheaper to recover from but does not make them rarer, and adds latency and cost.

prompt: A marketing team wants an assistant that writes product descriptions meeting a strict style guide. Drafts are usually close but fail a few rules, and a human currently fixes them by hand. The team can describe the rules precisely. Which pattern automates the fix-up most directly?

options.text: Routing: send each request to a different prompt depending on the product category it belongs to
Evaluator-optimizer: a checker tests the draft against the rules and the writer revises until it passes
Parallelisation: generate five drafts simultaneously and show the human reviewer all of them to choose between
Multi-agent: one specialist agent per style rule, each rewriting the draft for its own rule in turn

explanation: Correct: B. When evaluation criteria are clear and iteration demonstrably improves output, the evaluator-optimizer loop is the fit: generate, check against explicit rules, revise, with a bounded retry count. A changes who writes but not how violations get caught. C produces more drafts for the human to fix rather than fewer. D is far more machinery than a rules check needs and makes the rules interact unpredictably.

prompt: A logistics provider's leadership frames an AI programme around four pillars: efficiency, transformation, productivity and cost. The architect proposes an assistant that drafts customs declarations which clerks then check. Under which pillar should the business case primarily be made, and what metric supports it?

options.text: Transformation, measured by the number of new customer-facing services launched in the year
Cost, measured by the number of tokens consumed per customs declaration drafted
Efficiency, measured by clerk minutes per declaration and first-pass acceptance at customs
Performance SLA, measured by the model's p95 response latency on each declaration

explanation: Correct: C. Drafting for a human to check is an efficiency play on an existing process, and the honest metrics are the time saved per unit and whether quality held (acceptance rate). A describes a different kind of initiative that creates new offerings. B measures the solution's own running cost, not business value. D is a technical constraint to meet, not the reason to build it.

prompt: An agent that reconciles invoices against purchase orders occasionally runs for 40 tool calls on a single invoice before giving up, and a few runs have issued duplicate credit notes. The business accepts some manual fallback. Which pair of architectural controls should the architect add?

options.text: A longer system prompt explaining when to stop, plus a note asking the agent to avoid duplicate credit notes
A turn budget with a hand-off to a human queue, and an idempotency key on the credit-note tool
A second supervising agent that watches the first one's actions and intervenes when it misbehaves
Removing every tool that writes to the finance system and returning to a drafting-only assistant

explanation: Correct: B. Agents need engineered stopping conditions and safe tools: a turn budget with an explicit fallback bounds cost, and idempotent write tools make a retried or repeated action harmless. A relies on instructions to enforce what should be enforced by code. C adds a second non-deterministic component to police the first. D over-corrects; the business accepted automation with fallback, not the removal of it.

prompt: In the design of an end-to-end Claude solution, which component turns production outcomes into improvements to the system over time?

options.text: The input layer that validates and normalises incoming requests before processing begins
The processing layer where the model, retrieval and tools do the work of producing an answer
The output layer that formats and delivers results to the consuming system or user
The feedback loop that collects outcome signals and feeds evaluation and iteration

explanation: Correct: D. The exam guide frames architectures as input, processing, output and feedback loops; the feedback loop is the part that closes the cycle by turning real outcomes into evaluation data and prompt or design changes. A, B and C are each necessary, but none of them learns from what happened after the output was produced.

prompt: An architect is choosing between a fixed workflow and an autonomous agent for a new solution. Which TWO properties of the problem most strongly favour the fixed workflow? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The sequence of steps is the same for every request
The number of tool calls varies from one to dozens depending on what intermediate results show
Each step must be individually logged, validated and easy to replay
Requests are open-ended and the right approach is only discovered part-way through the work
The team expects the model to recover from unexpected tool errors by trying alternative approaches

explanation: Correct: A and C. A workflow is the right choice when the path is known up front and when the business needs step-level predictability, validation and replay. B, D and E describe variable, exploratory work where the model must decide its own next step, which is exactly what an agent loop is for.

prompt: A team is deciding whether a merger-screening task justifies a multi-agent design rather than one augmented agent. Which TWO characteristics of the task most strongly indicate that several agents are warranted? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Legal, financial and technical assessments each need their own tool set and specialist instructions
The whole task must finish in under two seconds to meet the agreed response-time target
The assessments can run independently and only need combining at the end
The task is a single extraction with a fixed schema applied to one document at a time
The budget per run is very small and every additional model call must be justified

explanation: Correct: A and C. Multiple agents pay off when sub-tasks need separate context and tools (so one agent's prompt would be bloated and confused) and when they can proceed in parallel and be merged. B and E argue against multi-agent, which adds latency and cost. D is a job for a single call.

prompt: A retailer wants to translate the problem "our returns desk is overwhelmed" into a Claude-based solution. Which TWO activities belong to translating the business problem before any architecture is chosen? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Mapping the current returns process to find where time and errors actually occur
Selecting the embedding model that will be used to index the product catalogue for retrieval
Defining what a successful outcome looks like and how it will be measured
Writing the first version of the system prompt for the returns-desk agent
Choosing between MCP and a direct API integration for connecting to the order system

explanation: Correct: A and C. Translating a business problem means understanding the process as it is and agreeing the measurable outcome; those decide what, if anything, to automate. B, D and E are design and implementation decisions that should follow from that understanding, not precede it.

prompt: A telecom classifies 600,000 short support messages a day into ten intents. On a labelled test set the smallest, middle and largest Claude models score within one point of each other, and the business cares about cost and latency. Which choice is best?

options.text: The largest model, because headroom for the occasional harder message justifies the extra cost
Alternate between the models on each request so that the average cost and latency even out
The middle model, as a reasonable compromise between capability and cost for a production system
The smallest model, since accuracy is equivalent on this task and it is the cheapest and fastest

explanation: Correct: D. Model selection is a trade-off driven by measured task performance: when evaluation shows no accuracy gap, the smaller model wins on both cost and latency at this volume. A pays for capability the data says is not needed. C compromises on a choice the evidence has already made. B adds variance in behaviour and latency for no benefit.

prompt: A legal-drafting feature needs to follow a 30-page playbook, reason about exceptions, and produce long documents, and it runs a few hundred times a day. The team is comparing the most capable Claude model with a mid-tier one. What should drive the decision?

options.text: Choose the mid-tier model as a rule; the capability difference rarely matters for drafting work in practice
Choose whichever model has the larger context window, since the playbook is 30 pages long
Run both on a representative evaluation set and weigh the quality gap against cost at this volume
Choose the most capable model, because legal drafting is important and errors are costly

explanation: Correct: C. The decision is an evidence-based trade-off: measure the quality gap on real examples, then decide whether it is worth the extra cost and latency at a few hundred runs a day, where the absolute cost difference is small. A and D decide on a rule of thumb instead of data. B picks on a dimension that may not differ between the candidates and does not measure the thing that matters.

prompt: An application's system prompt begins with the current date and time and the user's session ID, followed by 11,000 tokens of unchanging product policy, then the user turn. Prompt caching is enabled with a cache breakpoint after the policy, yet cache hits are almost zero. Why?

options.text: The policy section is too large to be cached in one block and must be split into smaller blocks
Caching matches an exact prefix, and the changing timestamp and session ID make every prefix unique
Cache hits only occur when the user message is identical between two consecutive requests
The cache breakpoint must be placed at the very start of the prompt rather than after the policy section

explanation: Correct: B. Prompt caching reuses a prefix that matches exactly up to the breakpoint. Dynamic values placed before the static content change the prefix on every request, so nothing is reusable; moving the timestamp and session ID after the policy (or into the user turn) restores hits. A is backwards: large static blocks are what caching is for. C is wrong because the user turn comes after the breakpoint and does not affect the cached prefix. D would cache nothing useful.

prompt: A team applied chain-of-thought prompting to every endpoint. A multi-step risk-assessment feature improved noticeably, but a simple endpoint that extracts an order number from a message is now slower and costlier with the same accuracy. What should the architect do?

options.text: Keep chain-of-thought on every endpoint for consistency across the platform's prompts
Remove chain-of-thought from the risk assessment as well, since it adds cost and latency there too
Keep chain-of-thought for the reasoning-heavy feature and use a direct prompt for the extraction
Replace chain-of-thought with few-shot examples on every endpoint, which are cheaper to run

explanation: Correct: C. Prompting techniques are chosen per task: step-by-step reasoning helps where there are steps to reason through, and is pure overhead on a lookup-style extraction. A pays for reasoning the extraction task does not use. B throws away a measured improvement. D changes technique uniformly again instead of matching technique to task.

prompt: A system prompt holds a non-negotiable rule ("do not disclose wholesale prices") in the middle of 14,000 tokens of product reference material. The rule is followed inconsistently, and rewording it has not helped. Which change is most likely to fix it?

options.text: Repeat the rule three times at different points inside the product reference material
Move the rule into a short delimited instructions section at the top, apart from the reference material
Raise the temperature so that the model weighs all parts of the prompt more evenly
Move the rule into the user turn on each request so that it is always the most recent instruction the model sees

explanation: Correct: B. Structure matters: instructions buried inside long reference content get diluted. Separating instructions from data with clear delimiters, placing critical rules prominently and restating them near the end is the standard structural fix. A adds noise without clear structure. C increases randomness, not adherence. D makes a system-level guardrail depend on each caller including it and leaves it exposed to user-side manipulation.

prompt: A reporting feature must emit output in an exact house format: fixed section order, named headings and a particular table layout. Prose instructions describing the format get it nearly right but not reliably. Which technique most directly fixes this?

options.text: Include two or three complete example outputs in the exact format as few-shot examples
Ask the model to think step by step about the required format before it starts writing
Switch to a larger model and keep the prose description of the format unchanged
Lower the maximum output tokens so that the model has less room to deviate from the format

explanation: Correct: A. Showing the format is more reliable than describing it: few-shot examples pin down structure, heading names and table layout in a way prose cannot. B helps reasoning tasks, not formatting. C may improve adherence somewhat but leaves the ambiguity of a prose spec in place. D truncates output rather than shaping it.

prompt: An assistant answers questions over a 180,000-token set of engineering standards by placing the whole set in context on every request. Answers about material in the middle of the set are noticeably weaker, and each request is slow and expensive. What is the best remedy?

options.text: Retrieve only the sections relevant to each question and place them, clearly labelled, in context
Keep the full set in context and add an instruction to pay particular attention to the middle sections
Split each request across two calls, each carrying half of the standards, and merge the two answers
Compress the standards by stripping all headings, numbering and whitespace to save tokens

explanation: Correct: A. Context window optimisation means putting the right tokens in, not all of them: retrieval cuts cost and latency and removes the mid-context quality dip by giving the model a focused, labelled set of sections. B instructs around a structural problem. C doubles the calls and still cannot say which half holds the answer. D saves a few tokens while destroying the structure the model uses to locate content.

prompt: Six teams in a company each maintain their own copy of a 2,000-token block of brand voice and compliance instructions inside their prompts. Updates are missed and the copies have drifted. Which prompt-reuse strategy addresses this?

options.text: Have each team shorten its own copy so that there is less text to keep in sync between them
Maintain the block as one versioned shared module that each team's prompt composes in at build time
Move the block into every user message so that the latest version is always the one in use
Fine-tune a company model on the brand voice so that the shared instruction block is no longer needed at all

explanation: Correct: B. Modular prompts treat shared instructions as a single, versioned component composed into each prompt, so one update reaches every team and drift stops. A reduces the size of the problem but not its cause. C still leaves six copies and wastes tokens on every turn. D is a heavyweight route to a maintainability problem and makes future updates slower, not faster.

prompt: An agent must apply a 9,000-token procedure for reconciling bank statements, but only about one request in twenty is a reconciliation. The team currently loads the procedure into every system prompt. Which approach keeps the capability while reducing per-request tokens?

options.text: Package the procedure as a Skill with a short description, loaded in full only when needed
Keep the procedure in every prompt but enable prompt caching so the repeated tokens are cheaper
Summarise the procedure to about 500 tokens and accept the loss of detail on the rare reconciliation request
Ask users to state up front whether their request is a reconciliation so the prompt can be chosen

explanation: Correct: A. Skills use progressive disclosure: the model sees only a brief description of each skill and loads the full instructions when they are relevant, so the 9,000 tokens are paid only on the one request in twenty that needs them. B lowers the price of the waste but still sends the tokens every time and consumes context. C sacrifices the detail a procedure exists to provide. D pushes a routing decision onto users.

prompt: A support assistant must stay within a defined scope and decline anything outside it. The team is designing a system prompt to act as that guardrail. Which design is most robust?

options.text: A single sentence asking the model to be helpful and to stay on topic with the customer
A prompt defining role and scope with examples and a refusal behaviour, plus an output check in code
A list of forbidden keywords in the system prompt that the model must not respond to
A system prompt that warns of penalties if the model strays from the defined support topics in any reply

explanation: Correct: B. A guardrail prompt is specific: role, explicit scope with examples of both sides, a defined refusal behaviour, and a check outside the model because a prompt alone can be talked around. A is too vague to be followed consistently. C is brittle and both over- and under-blocks. D does not change capability or scope and is not a reliable instruction technique.

prompt: A high-volume application has a large, mostly static prompt and rising per-request cost. Which TWO changes most directly cut cost per request without reducing capability? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Order the prompt so static content comes first and enable prompt caching on it
Delete the examples section and rely on the model to infer the required output format on its own
Route simple requests to a smaller model that evaluation shows performs equally on them
Increase the maximum output tokens so that fewer requests need a follow-up call to finish
Send each request twice to two models and keep whichever response turned out to be cheaper

explanation: Correct: A and C. Caching a stable prefix cuts the cost of the repeated tokens, and tiering requests to the smallest model that measurably does the job cuts cost where capability is not needed. B reduces tokens by removing something that was there for quality. D does not reduce input cost and may raise output cost. E doubles cost.

prompt: An architect is reviewing a system prompt that produces inconsistent behaviour. Which TWO practices are most likely to improve instruction adherence? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use clear delimiters or tags to separate instructions, reference data and examples
Write the instructions in as few words as possible, even where that leaves some cases implicit
Replace vague directives with explicit statements of the desired behaviour and its edge cases
Place the most important rule in the middle of the prompt where it is surrounded by supporting context
Raise the temperature so that the model handles varied inputs more flexibly and naturally

explanation: Correct: A and C. Clear structure (so the model can tell instructions from data) and explicit, specific instructions that cover the edge cases are the two highest-leverage fixes for inconsistency. B leaves cases implicit, which is where inconsistency comes from. D buries the rule. E increases variability.

prompt: A team wants a model to extract three fields from a short delivery note. The task is simple, the fields are unambiguous and the team has no labelled examples yet. Which prompting approach should they try first?

options.text: Zero-shot: a clear instruction naming the three fields and the output format
Chain-of-thought: ask the model to reason at length about the note before extracting
Few-shot: a twenty-example prompt built from synthetic delivery notes written by the team
Multi-agent: a pipeline with one agent per field, merged by an orchestrator at the end

explanation: Correct: A. Start simple: a precise zero-shot instruction is usually sufficient for an unambiguous extraction and is the cheapest to run and iterate on; add examples or reasoning only if evaluation shows a gap. B adds latency and tokens for a task with nothing to reason through. C front-loads effort on synthetic data before knowing it is needed. D is wildly over-engineered.

prompt: A company is connecting Claude to fifteen internal systems owned by different teams. Tools will be added and retired often, and several AI applications across the company need the same integrations. Which integration approach best fits?

options.text: Each application embeds its own direct API client for every one of the systems it needs
Applications call one another's agents to borrow the integrations they do not have themselves
One central team writes a single library containing all fifteen integrations and ships it to every application
Each system team publishes an MCP server for its system, and applications connect to the ones they need

explanation: Correct: D. MCP is designed for exactly this: a standard protocol in which each system is exposed once, by the team that owns it, and any number of model applications can discover and use it. A multiplies integration work by the number of applications. C centralises ownership away from the teams that know the systems and creates a release bottleneck. B couples applications to each other for no architectural reason.

prompt: An agent has grown to 52 registered tools across seven business areas. Tool-selection accuracy has fallen, latency has risen, and usage logs show that 20 of the tools have never been called in production. What should the architect do first?

options.text: Remove the unused tools, then group the rest so each request sees only its area's tools
Add more detailed descriptions to all 52 tools so that the model can tell them apart more reliably
Raise the model's maximum output tokens so that it can reason for longer about which tool to use
Move to the largest model available, which handles large tool sets more accurately than smaller ones

explanation: Correct: A. This is capability bloat: every registered tool costs tokens and dilutes selection on every call, so prune what is unused and scope what remains. B improves descriptions on tools that should not be there at all. C and D spend money on symptoms while the tool list keeps growing.

prompt: An assistant answers employees' questions about their own payroll records. It calls the payroll API with one service account that can read every employee's data, and the system prompt tells the model to return only the asking employee's records. A security review flags this. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Add a second instruction to the system prompt forbidding access to any other employee's data
Log every payroll query with the asking employee's ID so that any misuse can be detected and investigated afterwards
Pass the authenticated employee's identity to the tool layer and let the payroll API enforce the scope
Switch to a model that follows system-prompt instructions more reliably under adversarial input

explanation: Correct: C. Authorization must be enforced below the model, in the tool or API layer, using the caller's real identity; a prompt is not an access-control mechanism and can be manipulated. A and D keep the control in the prompt, which is the gap the review found. B is a detective control that catches disclosure after it has happened.

prompt: An HR onboarding agent was built on a generic "people operations" MCP server that exposes tools to view records, edit records, change salaries and terminate employment. The onboarding team only ever views and edits records. Applying least privilege, what should change?

options.text: Keep the full tool set but require a manager's confirmation before salary changes and terminations
Keep the full tool set and write every salary change and termination to an immutable audit log
Connect the agent only to the view and edit tools, leaving the other two unavailable to it
Add a system-prompt rule stating that the salary and termination tools must never be used by this agent

explanation: Correct: C. Least privilege means not granting a capability the role does not need; scoping the agent to the two tools it uses removes the risk rather than guarding it. A and B are compensating and detective controls that leave the dangerous capability in place. D relies on the model to decline a tool it has been given, which an injection or a mistake can override.

prompt: A RAG system over supplier contracts splits every document into fixed 250-token chunks. Retrieved chunks are often clause fragments whose meaning depends on definitions and cross-references elsewhere in the contract, and answers suffer. Which chunking change addresses this?

options.text: Reduce the chunks to 100 tokens so that retrieval becomes more precise about the matching clause
Chunk along clauses and sections, add overlap, and prepend document and section context to each chunk
Index each whole contract as a single chunk so that no clause is ever separated from its definitions
Keep the 250-token chunks but retrieve the top 50 instead of the top 5 so the context is more complete

explanation: Correct: B. Chunking should follow the shape of the data: structure-aware chunks with overlap and contextual headers keep a clause intact and tell the model which contract and section it came from. A makes the fragments smaller and worse. C produces chunks too large to retrieve precisely or fit several of in context. D floods the context with fragments instead of fixing them.

prompt: A spare-parts assistant uses purely semantic vector retrieval. Natural-language questions work well, but searches for exact part codes such as "TR-7731-C" often return similar-looking but wrong parts. Which retrieval strategy fixes this?

options.text: Replace the vector retrieval with keyword search only, since part codes are the harder case
Increase the embedding dimension so that codes like "TR-7731-C" are represented more precisely
Ask users to describe the part in words instead of entering codes, which embeddings handle well already
Hybrid retrieval: combine the semantic index with a lexical index so exact identifiers match

explanation: Correct: D. Retrieval should match the query pattern: embeddings capture meaning but not exact strings, while lexical search matches identifiers precisely, so combining the two serves both query types. A fixes codes but breaks the natural-language queries that currently work. B does not make embeddings exact-match. C works around the problem by changing user behaviour.

prompt: Adding a re-ranking step to a support assistant's retrieval raises answer accuracy from 85% to 92% and adds 600 ms. The contractual response-time SLA is 3 seconds and current p95 latency is 1.5 seconds. What should the architect decide?

options.text: Reject the re-ranker, because any added latency erodes the margin against the contractual SLA
Adopt the re-ranker: the gain is material, p95 stays inside the SLA, and record the decision
Adopt the re-ranker only for requests that arrive outside business hours when traffic is lower
Run the re-ranker asynchronously and update the answer on screen after it has already been shown to the user

explanation: Correct: B. An accuracy-latency trade-off is decided with numbers: a 7-point accuracy gain for 600 ms that leaves p95 at about 2.1 seconds against a 3-second SLA is a clear win, and the justification should be documented. A treats latency as the only metric. C makes quality depend on the clock. D shows users a worse answer first and complicates the experience for no latency reason.

prompt: A platform runs 80,000 agent sessions a day. Engineers log every full prompt, response and tool payload; storage cost is high and failures are still hard to locate. Which observability strategy is more appropriate at this scale?

options.text: Stop logging prompts and responses entirely and keep only aggregate error counts per day
Keep logging every prompt, response and tool payload in full but shorten retention to a single day to cut the storage bill
Structured traces per session with correlation IDs, step metadata, sampled payloads and full capture on failure
Log everything to a shared spreadsheet that engineers can filter and search by hand when needed

explanation: Correct: C. Observability at scale is about structure and sampling: traces that link every step of a session, metadata you can query, and full payloads only for a sample plus the failures you need to debug. A removes the information needed to diagnose anything. B keeps the cost problem and loses history. D does not scale past a few hundred sessions.

prompt: A hospital's scheduling agent must coordinate appointment slots with an independently operated transport provider's agent. Neither organisation will expose internal systems or tools to the other. Which connection mechanism fits?

options.text: The hospital agent is given direct API credentials for the transport provider's booking system
The transport provider publishes an MCP server exposing its internal tools for the hospital agent
An agent-to-agent protocol: the two agents exchange structured messages and keep their tools private
A shared database hosted by a third party that both organisations' agents read from and write to directly

explanation: Correct: C. When two autonomous agents under different ownership must cooperate without exposing internals, agent-to-agent communication is the mechanism: each side keeps its tools and systems behind its own agent and they exchange messages at the boundary. A and B expose one organisation's systems to the other's agent, which was ruled out. D is a tighter coupling than either organisation would accept.

prompt: An existing invoice-processing microservice needs to call Claude exactly once per document to classify it, inside its own tightly controlled pipeline with no need for the model to discover tools. Which integration mechanism is the most appropriate?

options.text: A direct Claude API call from the service with the document and the classification instructions
An MCP server wrapping the invoice service so that the model can discover and call it
An autonomous agent with the invoice service's functions registered as tools it may call
An agent-to-agent exchange between the invoice service and a separate classification agent run by another team

explanation: Correct: A. A single, deterministic model call inside existing application code is a direct API integration; MCP and agents add discovery and autonomy that this pipeline does not want. B inverts the direction: the service calls the model, not the other way round. C and D add planning and messaging overhead to a one-shot classification.

prompt: A knowledge agent could either load all 60 tool definitions and 30,000 tokens of reference material into every request, or load a short catalogue and fetch tool definitions and reference sections on demand. Requests are varied and most need two or three tools. Which strategy should the architect choose and why?

options.text: Monolithic context, because fetching on demand adds a round trip that the user would notice on every request
Progressive discovery, because most requests use a small fraction of the material
Monolithic context, because the model performs best when it can see all the tools and material at once
Progressive discovery, because it removes the need to maintain any tool descriptions at all

explanation: Correct: B. With varied requests that each use a small slice of a large tool and context set, progressive discovery wins: smaller prompts, less distraction, better selection, and the added lookup is cheap relative to the tokens saved. A overweights one extra round trip against a 30,000-token prompt. C is the opposite of what happens with large, mostly irrelevant context. D misdescribes the approach: a catalogue of short descriptions is still needed to choose what to load.

prompt: A RAG index is rebuilt nightly from a documentation site. After some rebuilds the assistant quotes superseded pages for part of the day. Which indexing practice addresses this most directly?

options.text: Rebuild the index every hour instead of every night so that superseded pages are replaced much sooner
Build the new index fully, switch to it atomically, and version each chunk's metadata
Instruct the model to prefer the content that sounds most recent whenever two retrieved chunks conflict
Retrieve more chunks per query so that the current version of a page is more likely to be included

explanation: Correct: B. Stale answers after a refresh come from serving a half-updated index or mixing old and new chunks; an atomic swap plus versioned metadata removes both causes. A makes the window of inconsistency more frequent rather than smaller. C asks the model to guess at freshness. D increases the chance of including stale chunks alongside current ones.

prompt: An agent has three tools named `search_docs`, `find_docs` and `lookup_docs` with similar one-line descriptions, and it frequently picks the wrong one. What should the architect change first?

options.text: Merge the overlapping tools and give each a distinct name and a description of when to use it
Add a fourth tool whose only job is to decide which of the three existing search tools should be called
Increase the number of retries so that the agent eventually lands on the right tool for the request
Present the three tools in a random order on each request to avoid any bias toward the first one

explanation: Correct: A. Tool selection is driven by names and descriptions: overlapping tools with vague descriptions are the root cause, so consolidate and describe precisely, including when not to use each. B adds a layer of indirection on top of the ambiguity. C makes errors slower and more expensive rather than rarer. D shuffles a problem it does not solve.

prompt: An internal MCP server exposes a `run_sql` tool that accepts arbitrary SQL against the analytics warehouse. The agent using it only ever needs monthly revenue by region. A security review asks for a change. Which is the best?

options.text: Keep `run_sql` but add a system-prompt rule that only SELECT statements may ever be issued
Replace `run_sql` with a narrow tool such as `revenue_by_region(month)` that runs a read-only query
Keep `run_sql` and log every statement it runs so that any misuse can be reviewed by the security team later
Keep `run_sql` and have the model confirm each query with the user before it is executed

explanation: Correct: B. A tool's interface defines the blast radius: a narrow, parameterised, read-only tool gives the agent exactly the capability it needs and nothing else, and it also improves selection and reliability. A puts a security boundary in the prompt. C detects misuse after the fact. D pushes the control onto the user and slows every request.

prompt: A new internal knowledge base should be usable by any current or future agent in the organisation without each agent team writing its own integration. Which mechanism serves this best?

options.text: A direct API call coded into each agent that needs to read from the knowledge base
A shared system prompt that includes the knowledge base contents for every agent to use
An MCP server for the knowledge base that any agent can connect to and discover
A nightly export of the knowledge base sent to each agent team to load however they prefer

explanation: Correct: C. Exposing a capability once, with discoverable tools and resources, for any model application to use is what MCP is for. A repeats the integration per agent. B does not scale and goes stale. D is not an integration at all.

prompt: A RAG assistant for a field-service company must answer two kinds of query: free-text questions about repair procedures, and lookups of a specific job by job number. Which TWO measures best match retrieval to these query patterns? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Use semantic retrieval for procedure questions and an exact-match lookup for job numbers
Use a single vector index for both and rely on the model to notice when a match is wrong
Attach metadata such as equipment type and date to chunks so retrieval can filter before ranking
Retrieve the top 100 chunks for every query so that the right one is always somewhere in context
Remove job numbers from the index entirely so that they cannot cause confusion in semantic search

explanation: Correct: A and C. Different query patterns call for different retrieval paths, and metadata filtering narrows the candidate set before semantic ranking. B leaves the exact-identifier weakness in place. D floods the context. E deletes the data needed for the lookup use case.

prompt: An architect is reviewing the authentication design of an agent that calls several internal APIs on behalf of users. Which TWO findings represent security gaps? (Select TWO.)

options.text: API keys for the internal systems are placed in the system prompt so the model can include them in tool calls
Tool calls are executed by application code that holds the credentials outside the model's context
The agent acts under one shared service identity regardless of which user is asking
Each tool call carries the end user's identity and the API enforces that user's own permissions
Credentials are rotated regularly and scoped to the minimum that each individual tool needs

explanation: Correct: A and C. Secrets in the prompt can be leaked in output or by injection, and a single shared identity means the API cannot enforce per-user permissions, so the model becomes the only access control. B, D and E are the correct practices: credentials held outside the model, user identity propagated to the enforcing layer, and least-privilege scoping.

prompt: An architect is weighing progressive discovery (loading tools and context on demand) against a monolithic strategy (everything in context up front). Which TWO situations most strongly favour progressive discovery? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The tool and reference set is large and any single request uses only a small part of it
Every request uses the same three tools and a 1,500-token prompt that rarely changes
New tools and documents are added often and must become available without redeploying the prompt
The system has a hard requirement of exactly one model call per request with no extra lookups
The whole context fits comfortably in the window and is fully covered by prompt caching

explanation: Correct: A and C. Progressive discovery pays off when the full set is large and sparsely used, and when the catalogue changes often, because on-demand loading keeps prompts small and lets new capabilities appear without prompt changes. B and E describe small, stable contexts where monolithic loading is simpler and cheaper. D rules out the extra lookup step that discovery needs.

prompt: A monitoring dashboard for a production agent shows average latency and total token spend per day. The team still cannot tell which step of a failing session went wrong. Which TWO additions would let them? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A correlation ID that links every model call and tool call in a session into one trace
A larger font and a clearer colour scheme on the dashboard's latency chart for readability
Per-step records of tool name, input summary, outcome and duration
A weekly email summarising total spend and request volume for the engineering managers
Removing tool-call logging altogether to reduce noise in the dashboards and cut storage

explanation: Correct: A and C. Diagnosing a failing session requires tracing: a session-level identifier that ties the steps together, and structured step-level records to inspect. B and D change presentation and reporting, not the information captured. E removes the very data needed.

prompt: A steering group asks whether a new policy-lookup assistant is "good enough to launch". The team has enthusiastic quotes from pilot users but no measurements. What should the architect put in place first?

options.text: A longer pilot with more users, so there are more quotes and anecdotes to present to the steering group
A dashboard of token spend and latency, which are the metrics the platform already emits
A larger model, so that the assistant's quality is less likely to be questioned at launch
Defined metrics for accuracy, latency, cost and safety, with launch thresholds agreed with the business

explanation: Correct: D. "Good enough" has to be defined before it can be measured: agree the metrics and the thresholds that count as ready, then measure against them. A collects more anecdotes. B measures what is easy rather than what matters, and leaves out accuracy and safety. C changes the system without being able to tell whether it got better.

prompt: A team is assembling an evaluation dataset for a travel-booking assistant before launch. Which composition gives the most trustworthy signal?

options.text: Two hundred synthetic conversations generated by the assistant's own model and graded automatically by that same model
The twenty conversations from the sales demo deck, since those are the ones stakeholders will try first
Real anonymised conversations plus hard, adversarial and edge cases, each with a reference answer
Whatever pilot users typed in the first week, without reference answers, graded by thumbs-up counts

explanation: Correct: C. A trustworthy evaluation set reflects real traffic, includes the hard and adversarial cases that break systems, and has reference answers and rubrics so grading is consistent. A measures the model against itself on data it generated. B is a tiny, flattering sample. D has no ground truth, so a confident wrong answer and a right one score the same.

prompt: A marketing-copy assistant must be checked for tone and brand alignment across thousands of outputs a week. Reviewing every output by hand is not feasible. Which evaluation method fits?

options.text: A model-as-judge grader with a written rubric, calibrated against a human-labelled sample
Exact string matching of each output against a bank of approved reference copy for the same product
A weekly review of ten randomly chosen outputs by the brand team, with no other automated checks
Measuring the average length of outputs, since on-brand copy tends to fall within a consistent length range

explanation: Correct: A. Tone and brand are subjective qualities that string matching cannot measure; a model grader working from a rubric scales to thousands of outputs, provided it is calibrated against human judgements and monitored for drift. B fails on any valid rewording. C covers a fraction of a percent of output and misses systematic problems. D measures a proxy with no real relation to tone.

prompt: A revised prompt beats the current production prompt by five points on the offline evaluation suite. The team wants confidence before replacing it for all users. What is the right next step?

options.text: Replace the production prompt immediately, because the offline suite is the agreed quality gate
Ask the pilot users which of the two prompts they prefer in a short survey before deciding
Re-run the offline suite several more times until the gap is statistically convincing, then deploy
Run an A/B test on a fraction of live traffic and compare the agreed metrics before full rollout

explanation: Correct: D. Offline gains do not always hold on live traffic; an A/B test on real requests with pre-agreed metrics is how the gain is confirmed, with a small blast radius if it does not hold. A skips the live check. C only tightens an offline estimate. B measures preference on a tiny sample rather than the agreed metrics on real traffic.

prompt: A finance director asks for a 40% cut in a solution's inference bill. The team's first proposal is to switch every workload to the smallest model. What should the architect do before agreeing?

options.text: Agree, since the cost target is a business decision and the smallest model is the fastest way to it
Refuse, since model downgrades always lower quality and the proposal should not be entertained
Profile the spend, then test cheaper options per workload against the evaluation suite
Switch only the most expensive workload to the smallest model and wait to see whether anyone complains

explanation: Correct: C. Cost optimisation starts by measuring where tokens go, then applies the cheapest change that holds quality, verified by evaluation; the smallest model may be right for some workloads and wrong for others. A and D change production without measuring quality. B rejects a reasonable goal instead of finding the safe route to it.

prompt: A team is moving production traffic to a newly released model version. Spot checks look fine. Which rollout practice best protects production quality?

options.text: Switch all traffic at once during a quiet period so that any problems surface quickly and at low volume
Run the evaluation suite on the new version, then roll out gradually with monitoring and a rollback path
Keep the old version indefinitely, since a system that is working should not be changed
Switch the staging environment only and leave production on the old version until users request the new one

explanation: Correct: B. A model change is a change to system behaviour: evaluate it against the suite, then expose it gradually with monitoring and rollback. A makes the whole user base the test. C ignores deprecation and improvement. D never completes the migration and gains no evidence about production behaviour.

prompt: An architect wants early warning of quality degradation in a production RAG assistant, before users start complaining. Which signal is the most useful leading indicator?

options.text: The number of support tickets that mention the assistant, reviewed by the team at the end of each month
Total monthly token spend compared with the budget that was approved for the assistant
The uptime percentage of the retrieval service and the vector database behind it
Retrieval quality on sampled live queries, such as relevance scores and unsupported answers

explanation: Correct: D. In a RAG system quality usually breaks at retrieval first, so monitoring retrieval relevance and unsupported answers on a live sample shows degradation before it reaches the user. A is a lagging indicator by definition. B tracks cost, not quality. C says the service is up, not that it returns the right chunks.

prompt: A summarisation feature using a small, fast model produces accurate summaries of short emails but consistently drops key points from 50-page reports, even with a well-structured prompt. Which system issue is this?

options.text: A hallucination, since the summaries contain content that the source reports do not actually contain
A prompt failure, since the instructions about completeness are not being followed
A retrieval failure, since the wrong parts of the long reports are being fetched
A model mismatch: the model copes with the short task but not the long, demanding one

explanation: Correct: D. The same prompt works on easy inputs and fails on hard ones, which points to the model's capability on long, dense documents rather than the prompt; the fix is a more capable model or decomposition. A describes invented content, but the problem here is omission. B is unlikely when the identical prompt succeeds on short inputs. C does not apply: there is no retrieval step.

prompt: A parcel-tracking assistant invents a plausible tracking number when the lookup tool returns no result, instead of telling the customer that nothing was found. What is the issue and the most direct fix?

options.text: A hallucination; define the empty-result behaviour and validate numbers against the tool output
A model mismatch; move to a larger model, which will know the correct tracking numbers for the parcels in question
A retrieval failure; add more parcels to the index so that the lookup tool returns a result more often
A latency issue; the tool is timing out and the model fills the gap, so increase the tool's timeout

explanation: Correct: A. Fabricating a value to fill a gap is a hallucination; the fix is to specify the empty-result behaviour in the prompt and to check output values against what the tool actually returned. B is wrong because no model knows tracking numbers it was not given. C misreads a correct empty result as a failure. D invents a cause the scenario does not describe.

prompt: An assistant told to "answer in two sentences" keeps producing long answers. Inspection of the system prompt finds a later section that says "explain your reasoning fully". Which issue is this?

options.text: A model mismatch, since a more capable model would reconcile the two instructions sensibly
A prompt failure from conflicting instructions: remove the contradiction and state the intent once
A hallucination, since the model is generating content that the user did not ask it to produce
A context-window problem, since the prompt is too long for the model to take all of it into account at once

explanation: Correct: B. Two instructions that cannot both be satisfied are a prompt defect; the model is following one of them. A asks a model to resolve an ambiguity the author should remove. C is wrong because the content is relevant, just too long. D is not indicated by anything in the scenario.

prompt: A document-analysis pipeline's p95 latency is 9 seconds. Tracing shows three sequential model calls of about 2.5 seconds each plus a 1.5-second retrieval step, and the second and third calls do not depend on each other. Which optimisation gives the largest latency reduction without changing quality?

options.text: Run the second and third calls in parallel, cutting about 2.5 seconds from the critical path
Enable prompt caching on all three calls, which will make each of them return almost instantly
Move all three calls to the smallest model to roughly halve the time taken by each one
Remove the retrieval step and rely on the model's own knowledge of the documents instead

explanation: Correct: A. The trace shows two independent calls run in sequence; parallelising them removes a whole call from the critical path with no change to outputs. B reduces time-to-first-token on cached prefixes but does not eliminate generation time. C changes quality, which the question rules out. D removes grounding and will change answers.

prompt: A nightly job classifies 300,000 documents. Results are needed by the next morning and nobody waits on an individual document. Which change most reduces cost without changing the model or the prompt?

options.text: Run the requests through the synchronous API with higher concurrency so the job finishes sooner
Shorten every document to its first paragraph before classification to cut the input tokens
Retry each request several times and keep the cheapest response that comes back from the model
Submit the documents through the batch API, trading latency the job does not need for a lower price

explanation: Correct: D. Batch processing is the designed trade: asynchronous completion within a window in exchange for a lower price, which fits a nightly job with no interactive user. A finishes faster but does not cost less. B changes the inputs and therefore the results. C makes no sense: pricing is per token, and retries add cost.

prompt: A team is defining metrics for an internal HR assistant. Which set covers the dimensions the exam blueprint expects an evaluation plan to address?

options.text: Accuracy only, since an assistant that gives correct answers is by definition a good one
Accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security, each with a target and a way to measure it
Latency and cost, because those are the two metrics the platform reports automatically
User satisfaction score alone, because the users of the assistant are the final judges

explanation: Correct: B. An evaluation plan covers accuracy, latency, cost, safety and security together, each with a measurable target; optimising one in isolation hides regressions in the others. A ignores whether the system is affordable, fast enough or safe. C ignores whether it is right. D is useful but lagging, subjective and silent on safety and cost.

prompt: A team is designing the pre-production evaluation framework for an assistant that will operate in a regulated industry. Which TWO components are most important to include? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A held-out test set with reference answers that the prompt was never tuned against
A demo script that shows the assistant's best answers to executives and the regulator's liaison
Human expert review of a stratified sample, including safety and compliance cases, plus automated grading
A single aggregate quality score so that the results are simple to communicate to leadership
Evaluation run only on the final day before launch so that the results reflect the shipped version

explanation: Correct: A and C. A regulated setting needs a clean held-out set (so scores are not inflated by tuning) and expert human review on the risky categories, combined with automated grading for scale. B is marketing, not evaluation. D hides the per-category failures a regulator will ask about. E leaves no time to act on the findings.

prompt: A production assistant's answer quality has degraded intermittently over two weeks. Latency, model version and prompts are unchanged. Which TWO data sources are most useful for finding the cause? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Traces of failing sessions showing which chunks were retrieved and which tools were called
The total number of requests per day over the two weeks, broken down by hour and by channel
The change history of the retrieval index and its source documents over the same period
The team's on-call roster showing who was responsible for the system on each of the days
The model provider's public status page and its incident history for the two-week period

explanation: Correct: A and C. With model, prompt and latency ruled out, the moving parts are the data and the tools: session traces show what the model was given, and the index change history shows whether the inputs changed when quality did. B and D are unlikely to explain an intermittent quality change. E matters for outages, not gradual degradation with an unchanged model.

prompt: A team wants to reduce token usage on a long-running support conversation without harming answer quality. Which TWO techniques apply? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Summarise or compact older turns past a length threshold, keeping the facts the assistant still needs
Delete the system prompt after the first turn, since the model will remember it for the session
Prune large tool results from earlier turns once used, leaving a short note of what was found
Send the full conversation twice per turn to be sure that nothing important is lost
Replace every tool result with the word "done" the moment it is returned to save tokens

explanation: Correct: A and C. Context management for long sessions means compacting history and clearing bulky tool outputs once they have served their purpose, while preserving the information still needed. B breaks the assistant: each request is stateless and the system prompt must be sent every time. D doubles cost. E destroys information before it is used.

prompt: An agent can draft supplier emails, update internal records and raise purchase orders up to 40,000 euros. The business wants human oversight without slowing every interaction. Where should the human approval gate go?

options.text: Before every action the agent takes, so that nothing at all happens without a person seeing it first
Nowhere; the agent's spending limit of 40,000 euros is itself a sufficient control
After each purchase order is sent, as part of a weekly review of all the orders the agent raised
Before irreversible or costly actions such as raising a purchase order; drafting and updates run free

explanation: Correct: D. Human-in-the-loop gates belong where the consequence is high and hard to undo; low-risk, reversible actions can flow freely. A defeats the purpose of automation. B treats a spending cap as oversight, which it is not. C reviews after the money has been committed.

prompt: A European retailer's assistant sends complete customer chats, including names and addresses, to a third-party analytics service outside the EU for quality monitoring. The data protection officer objects under GDPR. Which architectural change best answers the objection?

options.text: Add a line to the privacy policy stating that chats may be analysed by a provider outside the EU for quality purposes
Keep sending the full chats but encrypt them in transit and at rest with the analytics provider
Pseudonymise or strip personal data before export, send only what monitoring needs, cover the transfer
Stop quality monitoring entirely so that no customer data ever leaves the retailer's own systems

explanation: Correct: C. GDPR compliance in the architecture means data minimisation and lawful transfer: remove or pseudonymise personal data before it leaves, send only the fields monitoring needs, and put a valid transfer basis in place. A is a notice, not a safeguard. B protects the channel but still exports personal data. D removes a needed capability instead of making it compliant.

prompt: A hospital wants an assistant that answers clinicians' questions using patient records. Which consideration must be settled at the architecture stage rather than left for a later release?

options.text: The colour scheme and layout of the interface that clinicians will use on the wards and in clinics
How protected health information flows end to end: storage, processing, access and audit under HIPAA
Which emoji the assistant uses when it acknowledges a question from a clinician
The wording of the welcome message that is shown to each clinician on first use

explanation: Correct: B. Regulated data flows are structural: where protected health information goes, which services touch it, access control and audit logging cannot be bolted on after launch without rebuilding the system. A, C and D are presentation details that can change at any time without affecting compliance.

prompt: A tenant-screening assistant is found to rate applicants from certain neighbourhoods systematically lower, even though names and demographic fields were removed from its input. What does this most likely indicate, and what should be done?

options.text: The model is malfunctioning; restart the deployment and re-run all the affected applications through it again
The removed fields were not the problem; add them back so that the model has fuller context
A proxy such as postcode encodes a protected trait; audit inputs, measure outcomes by group, add fairness tests
The result is a statistical coincidence and no action is required until more data has been collected

explanation: Correct: C. Removing explicit demographic fields does not remove bias when other inputs act as proxies; the response is to find the proxies, measure outcomes by group and make fairness a standing part of evaluation. A treats a data problem as an outage. B reintroduces the direct features. D ignores a systematic disparity with legal and ethical consequences.

prompt: A security test of a document-assistant shows that text inside a retrieved PDF can change the assistant's behaviour: a planted instruction to reveal the system prompt partly succeeded. What is the correct architectural response?

options.text: Treat retrieved content as untrusted data: delimit it, say it holds no instructions, and enforce limits in code
Add a line to the system prompt saying the model must ignore any instructions found in documents, then close the issue
Scan incoming documents for the phrase "ignore previous instructions" and reject any document that contains it
Stop retrieving documents altogether and rely on the model's training knowledge to answer questions

explanation: Correct: A. Indirect prompt injection is a trust-boundary problem: content from outside is data, not instructions, and the real limits on what the system can do must be enforced in code regardless of what the model is persuaded to say. B relies on the prompt alone, which the test already showed is insufficient. C blocks one phrasing of an unbounded set. D removes the product's core capability.

prompt: An insurer deploys an AI assistant on its public website. Compliance asks how the design supports transparency obligations. Which measure addresses this most directly?

options.text: Making the assistant's replies sound as human as possible so that customers feel comfortable
Keeping the system prompt confidential so that competitors cannot copy the assistant's behaviour or tone
Using the largest available model so that the assistant's answers are more often correct
Disclosing that the customer is talking to an AI, stating its limits, and offering a route to a human

explanation: Correct: D. Transparency means users know they are dealing with an AI, understand what it can and cannot do, and can reach a person; this is what regulators and ethical guidelines ask for. A works against transparency. B is about confidentiality, not transparency. C is about accuracy, which is a different obligation.

prompt: A customer-service assistant must never include a customer's full card number in any reply, regardless of what the customer or a retrieved document says. Which control is the primary one?

options.text: A system-prompt instruction asking the model to be careful when handling card numbers
A human review of every reply before it is sent to the customer, regardless of content
A monthly audit of a random sample of sent replies to check whether any of them contain card numbers
A deterministic output filter outside the model that detects card-number patterns and redacts them

explanation: Correct: D. A hard "never" rule on a pattern that can be detected deterministically belongs in an output guardrail enforced in code; it works even when the model is manipulated. A is a soft control that can be overridden. C finds leaks a month later. B works but is disproportionate for a rule a regex can enforce.

prompt: A lending assistant produces loan-approval recommendations, each of which has significant financial and regulatory consequences. Which control should be primary?

options.text: An output filter that blocks any recommendation containing certain high-risk words or phrases
A dashboard showing the approval and rejection rates over time, reviewed by the risk team
A human decision-maker who reviews and owns each recommendation before it takes effect
A more detailed system prompt that describes the lending policy and its exceptions in full

explanation: Correct: C. For high-stakes, regulated decisions the primary control is human validation: the model recommends and a person decides. A catches surface patterns, not bad judgements. B is monitoring, which detects trends after decisions have been made. D improves inputs but leaves the model as the decision-maker.

prompt: Compliance must be able to show, months after the event, exactly what an agent did and why during a disputed transaction. Which control provides this?

options.text: A human approval step before each transaction the agent processes, recorded in the approval tool
An output filter applied to every reply the agent sends to the customer during the transaction
A rate limit on how many transactions the agent can process in any one hour, enforced by the gateway
An immutable, timestamped audit log of each step, tool call, input and decision, retained as required

explanation: Correct: D. Reconstructing a past decision needs a complete, tamper-evident record of the agent's steps kept for as long as regulation requires. A prevents some bad actions but does not record reasoning. B filters output rather than recording it. C limits volume and says nothing about any individual transaction.

prompt: A government agency wants to use a Claude-based assistant for internal case work and asks whether the deployment can meet FedRAMP requirements. What is the architect's correct first step?

options.text: Confirm the model and platform are offered in a FedRAMP-authorised environment and keep data inside it
Add a disclaimer to the assistant stating that it must not be used for sensitive or classified case data of any kind
Assume any cloud deployment is acceptable because the model provider is a large and well-known company
Run the model on employees' laptops so that the agency avoids cloud compliance obligations altogether

explanation: Correct: A. FedRAMP compliance is a property of the authorised environment: the architect must verify the platform's authorisation and keep the data within that boundary. B does not change where the data goes. C substitutes reputation for authorisation. D is neither possible for a hosted model nor a compliance strategy.

prompt: A product owner proposes that a Claude assistant give final answers on medication dosages to patients with no clinician involved, because "the model is very accurate". Which limitation of LLM systems most directly argues against this design?

options.text: LLMs cannot read numbers reliably, so dosages will be garbled in the answers they give to patients
LLMs are slower than a human pharmacist at answering dosage questions
LLMs can give confident, fluent answers that are wrong, so high-harm domains need human validation
LLMs cannot be used in healthcare at all under current regulation in any jurisdiction, so the design is illegal

explanation: Correct: C. The relevant failure mode is confident error: fluency is not accuracy, and where a wrong answer can cause serious harm the design needs human-in-the-loop validation. A and B are false. D overstates the position; healthcare use is possible with appropriate controls.

prompt: A bank is deploying an assistant that drafts replies to customer complaints. Regulators require that no incorrect financial commitment reaches a customer. Which TWO controls most directly meet this requirement? (Select TWO.)

options.text: A system prompt asking the model to be careful and accurate about all financial matters
Human review and sign-off of every draft before it is sent
A larger model, which makes fewer factual mistakes when drafting replies
A deterministic check that flags any draft containing amounts, dates or commitments for verification
A faster response-time target so that customers receive replies to their complaints sooner

explanation: Correct: B and D. A "none may reach the customer" requirement calls for hard controls: a person accountable for each outgoing reply, and an automated check that catches commitments for verification. A and C reduce the error rate but cannot guarantee zero. E is unrelated to the requirement.

prompt: An architect is hardening a RAG agent with write tools against prompt injection carried in retrieved documents. Which TWO measures most reduce the risk? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Limit the agent's tools to the minimum needed and require confirmation for writes
Ask the model to rate how trustworthy each retrieved document seems before deciding whether to use it
Delimit retrieved content and tell the model it is data that may contain adversarial text
Increase the number of retrieved chunks per query so that any injected text is diluted by the rest
Disable logging of retrieved content so that injected text is never stored in the trace system

explanation: Correct: A and C. Defence in depth against injection combines reducing what a hijacked model can do (least privilege, confirmations on consequential actions) with making the trust boundary explicit in the prompt. B asks the model to police itself. D adds more untrusted text. E hampers investigation and prevents nothing.

prompt: A team is listing the risks of a new customer-facing assistant for a risk register. Which TWO are genuine LLM-system failure modes that belong on the register? (Select TWO.)

options.text: The model fabricates a policy clause that does not exist in the source documents
